# Predicting Voluntary Insurance Enrollment — Report

**Author:** Vicky Kumar Maurya
**Dataset:** `employee_data.csv` — 10,000 synthetic employee records, 9 features, binary target `enrolled`
**Code:** all figures and numbers in this report are regenerated by `make eda && make train`

---

## Headline finding, stated up front

**The target is a deterministic function of four features. There is no noise in this dataset, and no irreducible error.** I recovered the exact generating rule, which reproduces all 10,000 labels with **zero mismatches**:

```
enrolled = 1  ⟺  at least 3 of the following 4 conditions hold:

      age > 30                       salary > 60,000
      employment_type == "Full-time" has_dependents == "Yes"
```

Everything else in this report should be read in that light. The models score a perfect **1.000 ROC-AUC on the held-out test set** — not because the modelling is unusually good, but because the label is a closed-form rule that a depth-4 decision tree can represent exactly. `tenure_years`, `gender`, `marital_status` and `region` are **noise by construction**; they appear nowhere in the rule, and permutation importance assigns them exactly 0.0000.

I want to be direct about what this means for the exercise: **a 100% accurate model here is evidence about the data generator, not about the method.** The genuinely useful work was detecting that, and Section 5 covers what I would do differently if this were a real enrollment problem.

### How the rule was found

`src/eda.py::discover_generating_rule` runs this automatically on every EDA pass:

1. Fit an **unconstrained decision tree on the entire dataset**. It reaches 100% training accuracy at **depth 5 with 13 leaves**. A shallow, tiny tree separating every row perfectly means the label carries no stochastic component — with real behavioural data this is essentially impossible, and it is a signal to stop and check the data rather than celebrate the metric.
2. Given determinism, search `at least k of n` rules over the threshold conditions the univariate analysis suggested. Exactly one rule reproduces the label perfectly.

This check is cheap, and it is the check that separates "my model is excellent" from "my data is synthetic". I would run it on any suspiciously strong result.

---

## 1. Data observations

### 1.1 Quality

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Rows / columns | 10,000 × 10 |
| Missing values | **None**, in any column |
| Duplicate `employee_id` | 0 |
| Duplicate records | 0 |
| Categorical levels | ≤ 4 per feature, no unexpected values |
| Target balance | **61.7% enrolled / 38.3% not** |

The class balance is mild. I deliberately did **not** apply SMOTE or resampling: at 62/38 the minority class has ~3,800 examples, resampling would distort the probability calibration that the cost analysis in Section 4 depends on, and `class_weight="balanced"` was available to the search where it helped.

**Two defects worth flagging.**

- **385 rows (3.9%) have `tenure_years` greater than `age − 18`** — an impossible working history, e.g. a 25-year-old with 20 years of service. These are kept, not dropped and not overwritten. There is no ground truth to correct them to, and `tenure` carries no signal anyway, so dropping 3.9% of rows would cost information on the four features that *do* matter, in exchange for nothing. Instead `FeatureEngineer` derives `tenure_ratio = tenure_years / max(age − 18, 1)`, where any value above 1.0 marks the anomaly and makes it available to the model rather than hiding it.
- **`salary` has a floor of $2,208 on a full-time record**, and the salary distribution is statistically identical across `employment_type` (Full-time mean $65,108, Part-time $64,756, Contract $65,053). In real payroll data part-time salaries would be markedly lower. This is one of several tells that the data is synthetic.

### 1.2 Signal

Enrollment rate by feature — the entire structure of the problem is visible here:

| Feature | Enrollment rate | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| `employment_type` | Full-time **75.3%** · Contract 31.2% · Part-time 28.5% | Strong |
| `has_dependents` | Yes **79.7%** · No 34.8% | Strong |
| `age` | ≤30: **26.4%** → >30: ~70% at every band above | **Step, not a slope** |
| `salary` | <$62k: ~35% → >$62k: ~79% | **Step, not a slope** |
| `tenure_years` | 60.8%–62.2% across all quintiles | Flat — no signal |
| `region` | 61.2%–62.8% across all four | Flat — no signal |
| `gender` | 61.6%–64.3% | Flat — no signal |
| `marital_status` | 60.0%–62.9% | Flat — no signal |

The two step functions are the modelling crux. `age` and `salary` correlate with the target at 0.269 and 0.366 — moderate numbers that badly understate their importance, because Pearson correlation measures *linear* association and the true effect is a cliff edge. **Judging these features by correlation alone would have underrated both.**

![Enrollment rate by feature](artifacts/figures/eda_target_relationships.png)

## 2. Modelling approach

### 2.1 Design principles

**Everything sits inside one `sklearn.Pipeline`.** Imputation, scaling and encoding are fitted *within* each cross-validation fold, so no statistic from a validation fold leaks into preprocessing. Fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting is the most common silent error in take-home submissions, and it inflates scores in a way nothing downstream will catch.

**`employee_id` is dropped.** It is a surrogate row identifier; keeping it invites memorisation and offers nothing.

**Feature engineering is deliberately minimal** — `log_salary` and `tenure_ratio`, each with a stated reason. I specifically did *not* hand-code `age > 30` or `salary > 60000` as features. Having discovered the rule during EDA, encoding it directly would be leaking analysis into the feature set and would prove nothing about the pipeline. Letting the trees find the cuts themselves, and then showing the recovered thresholds in the partial-dependence plots, is stronger evidence.

### 2.2 Candidates and rationale

| Model | Why it is in the comparison | CV ROC-AUC |
|---|---|---|
| `DummyClassifier` | Majority-class floor. Anchors the reader: 61.7% accuracy is what "predict everyone enrolls" scores. | 0.5000 |
| Logistic regression | Interpretable baseline; predicted to underfit the step functions. | 0.9691 |
| Logistic + quantile binning | Same estimator, binned numerics — isolates representation from capacity. | 0.9991 |
| Decision tree (depth-tuned) | Axis-aligned splits match threshold rules exactly; readable by a non-technical stakeholder. | **0.9997** |
| Random forest | Standard non-linear reference. | 1.0000 |
| Histogram gradient boosting | Expected top performer. | 1.0000 |

*5-fold stratified CV on the training split, tuned by `RandomizedSearchCV` (30 candidates per model), scored on ROC-AUC.*

**The binned-logistic result is the most informative row in the table.** Plain logistic regression reaches 0.9691; the identical estimator with quantile-binned numerics reaches 0.9991, closing ~97% of the gap to the tree models. That confirms the baseline was limited by *feature representation*, not model capacity — the linear-in-log-odds assumption cannot express a cliff at age 30, but a linear model over binned features can. This is exactly the diagnosis the comparison was designed to produce.

![Model comparison](artifacts/figures/model_comparison.png)

### 2.3 Why a decision tree was selected

Random forest and gradient boosting both score a perfect 1.0000. The pipeline nonetheless selects the **decision tree** (depth 4, `min_samples_leaf=10`, entropy, balanced class weights), via a **one-standard-error rule**: among models within one standard error of the best CV score, take the simplest.

The tree scores 0.9997 against 1.0000 — a gap of 0.0003, which on a 2,000-row test set is roughly *half an employee's worth of ranking*. Paying for that with 300 trees, an unreadable decision surface and ~30× the training time is a bad trade. The tree is auditable by a compliance reviewer, scores in microseconds, and — as it turns out — represents the true rule exactly.

One caveat on my own method: because the top models score identically on every fold, their standard error collapses to exactly zero, which would make the one-SE rule demand a perfect tie. I therefore floor the tolerance at 0.0005 ROC-AUC (`config.SELECTION_MIN_DELTA`). That constant is a judgement call and I would rather name it than bury it.

### 2.4 Feature-engineering ablation

Running the full comparison with `--no-feature-engineering`:

| Model | With engineered features | Without | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Logistic | 0.9691 | 0.9665 | **+0.0026** |
| Logistic (binned) | 0.9991 | 0.9990 | +0.0001 |
| Decision tree | 0.9997 | 0.9997 | 0.0000 |
| Random forest | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.0000 |
| Hist. gradient boosting | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.0000 |

**The engineered features are worth almost nothing here**, and only to the plain linear model — `log_salary` slightly linearises a skewed predictor, which is exactly the model that needed help. Trees are invariant to monotonic transforms, so the result is unsurprising, but I would rather report a measured null result than assume the features earned their place. They stay in because `tenure_ratio` documents a real data defect, and because the cost is zero.

## 3. Results

Held-out test set (2,000 rows, stratified, used exactly once):

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| ROC-AUC | **1.0000** |
| PR-AUC | **1.0000** |
| Accuracy | 1.0000 |
| Precision / Recall / F1 | 1.0000 / 1.0000 / 1.0000 |
| Brier score | 0.0000 |
| Confusion matrix | TN 765 · FP 0 · FN 0 · TP 1,235 |

To restate Section 0: **these numbers describe the dataset, not the modelling.** A perfect score on real enrollment data would mean a leaked feature; here it means a deterministic generator.

![ROC and PR curves](artifacts/figures/roc_pr_curves.png)

### 3.1 What the model learned

Permutation importance on the test set is a clean confirmation of the recovered rule:

| Feature | Drop in ROC-AUC when shuffled |
|---|---|
| `has_dependents` | 0.2298 |
| `salary` | 0.2209 |
| `employment_type` | 0.1892 |
| `age` | 0.1408 |
| `region` | **0.0000** |
| `marital_status` | **0.0000** |
| `gender` | **0.0000** |
| `tenure_years` | **0.0000** |

The four rule features carry all the signal; the four noise features are *exactly* zero, to four decimals. I used permutation importance rather than impurity-based importance on purpose — the latter is biased toward continuous and high-cardinality features and would have given `tenure_years` and `salary` spurious credit.

The partial-dependence curves show the model independently recovering the thresholds at **age ≈ 30** and **salary ≈ $60,000**, with a flat line for `tenure_years`:

![Partial dependence](artifacts/figures/partial_dependence.png)

### 3.2 Robustness across subgroups

Performance by `gender`, `region` and `employment_type` is identical (ROC-AUC 1.000, recall 1.000) across every slice. This is a genuine negative result and worth stating plainly: the model is not disadvantaging any subgroup — but only because those attributes are noise in a synthetic generator. **On real data this check would be the one most likely to fail**, and it would need to run before any deployment, not after. `gender` in particular should be reviewed for legal admissibility in an insurance context regardless of whether it improves the metric.

---

## 4. The decision threshold is a business choice, not a modelling one

A ranked score is not a decision. Turning "0.73" into "contact this person" requires knowing what each kind of error costs. **I have no real economics for this product, so I state my assumption openly** (`src/config.py`):

- **False positive** — contacting someone who was never going to enroll: **$25** in wasted outreach.
- **False negative** — missing someone who would have enrolled: **$300** in forgone first-year margin.

Only the 12:1 ratio matters. For a calibrated model the cost-optimal threshold is `cost_FP / (cost_FP + cost_FN)` = **0.077**, and the empirical sweep confirmed it (0.074) on an earlier, imperfect model. **The business implication is more interesting than the number: when missing a customer costs 12× more than a wasted call, you should contact almost everyone with any meaningful probability.** On that earlier model the tuned threshold cut cost per employee from $19.62 to $3.34 — an 83% reduction — while accuracy *fell* from 90.3% to 87.8%.

That trade is the entire argument for not optimising accuracy. A model tuned to look good on accuracy would have cost roughly six times more to operate.

On the final perfect model this analysis degenerates: classes are perfectly separated, so every threshold between the two score clusters costs zero and the sweep reports the midpoint (0.501). The machinery is in place and tested (`tests/test_evaluate.py`) for the moment the data is real.

![Threshold analysis](artifacts/figures/threshold_analysis.png)

## 5. Key takeaways and next steps

### Takeaways

1. **The dataset is deterministic and fully solved.** Enrollment = at least 3 of {age > 30, salary > $60k, full-time, has dependents}, verified on all 10,000 rows. Any model flexible enough to represent axis-aligned thresholds reaches 100%.
2. **A perfect score is a red flag, not a trophy.** The most valuable step in this exercise was testing whether the target was noiseless before interpreting any metric.
3. **Correlation understated the two most important numeric features**, because their effects are steps rather than slopes. The binned-logistic experiment quantified this: representation, not capacity, was the binding constraint.
4. **The simplest adequate model won.** A depth-4 tree matched a 300-tree forest to within 0.0003 AUC, and is auditable.
5. **Half the features are noise by construction** — confirmed independently by permutation importance at exactly zero.

### Next steps

**If this dataset were the real thing (it is not):**
- Ship the decision tree, or frankly ship the rule itself as four lines of business logic — an ML model is not needed to evaluate a 3-of-4 threshold rule. Recommending the simpler non-ML solution is part of an honest recommendation.
- Drop `tenure_years`, `gender`, `region` and `marital_status` from collection; they cost privacy and compliance exposure for zero signal.

**To make this a real enrollment model:**
- **Get real data.** Everything above is method demonstration; none of the coefficients or thresholds transfer.
- **Add the features that plausibly drive the actual decision** and are absent here: premium cost, employer contribution %, plan alternatives, prior-year enrollment, open-enrollment timing, tenure at the *decision date* rather than today. Enrollment is a price-sensitive decision and there is no price in this dataset.
- **Fix the temporal framing.** Features and target must be separated by a decision date, with a time-based split rather than a random one, or the model will train on facts that postdate the choice it is predicting.
- **Re-run the fairness slices for real.** With genuine data these would not come back flat, and `gender` may not be legally usable at all.
- **Monitor for drift** on the input distributions and on the enrollment rate; recalibrate the threshold as the true cost ratio becomes measurable from campaign results.
- **Replace the assumed cost ratio with measured economics** from an outreach A/B test — the threshold, and therefore the operating cost, depends entirely on it.

## Appendix — reproducing this report

```bash
make setup    # virtualenv + pinned dependencies
make eda      # data-quality report, rule discovery, EDA figures
make train    # tuning, selection, held-out evaluation, artifacts
make test     # 76 tests
```

Every number quoted above is written to `artifacts/metrics/metrics.json` and `artifacts/metrics/eda_summary.json`, and every figure to `artifacts/figures/`. Runs are seeded (`--seed`, default 42) and reproducible.
